t: Subsequences with a Unique Middle Mode — Case Analysis Over the Middle Index
o: Count 5-element subsequences whose middle element (3rd smallest index) is the unique most frequent value. Fix the middle index i with value v; a valid subsequence takes exactly 2 elements from the left of i and 2 from the right. If a of the left picks and b of the right picks equal v, then v occurs m = 1+a+b times, and every other value may occur at most m-1 times. Enumerating (a,b) and counting non-v picks with per-value caps — using a small polynomial product for the tightest case m=2 — yields an O(n^2) algorithm. Verified on the samples: [1,2,2,3,3,4] gives 4, all-ones gives 6.
k: Fixing the middle index forces exactly 2 picks on each side, turning the problem into capped selection counts from left/right multisets.

For m >= 3 the per-value cap (m-1 >= 2) is never binding because only <= 2 non-v slots exist, so closed-form binomials suffice; only m=2 (all non-v distinct) needs the polynomial product Π(1 + Lx·x + Rx·y) truncated at degree 2.

a.n: Approach 1: Middle Enumeration with Polynomial Counting
a.i: For each middle index i, build left/right value counters, extract v's counts (Lv, Rv) and non-v totals (A, B). Multiply the per-value linear factors (1 + Lx·x + Rx·y) into a 3x3 truncated grid p, where p[a][b] counts ways to pick a non-v elements on the left and b on the right with all values distinct. Then sum the seven (a,b) cases: m=2 uses p, m=3/4/5 use binomials, since caps of 2+ are automatic with at most 2 slots per side.
s: For each i: build counters L, R; remove v to get Lv, Rv, A, B.
Compute p = Π over non-v values of (1 + Lx·x + Rx·y), truncated to degrees <= 2 in each variable.

c.python:
class Solution:
    def countSubsequences(self, nums: List[int]) -> int:
        MOD = 10**9 + 7
        n = len(nums)
        ans = 0
        for i in range(n):
            v = nums[i]
            L = {}; R = {}
            for j in range(i): L[nums[j]] = L.get(nums[j], 0) + 1
            for j in range(i+1, n): R[nums[j]] = R.get(nums[j], 0) + 1
            Lv = L.pop(v, 0); Rv = R.pop(v, 0)
            A = sum(L.values()); B = sum(R.values())
            p = [[0]*3 for _ in range(3)]
            p[0][0] = 1
            for k in set(L) | set(R):
                lx = L.get(k, 0); rx = R.get(k, 0)
                q = [[0]*3 for _ in range(3)]
                for a in range(3):
                    for b in range(3):
                        c = p[a][b]
                        if c:
                            q[a][b] += c
                            if a < 2: q[a+1][b] += c * lx
                            if b < 2: q[a][b+1] += c * rx
                p = q
            c2 = lambda x: x * (x - 1) // 2
            t = (Lv * p[1][2] + Rv * p[2][1]
                 + c2(Lv) * c2(Rv)
                 + c2(Lv) * Rv * B + Lv * c2(Rv) * A
                 + c2(Lv) * c2(B) + c2(A) * c2(Rv) + Lv * Rv * A * B)
            ans = (ans + t) % MOD
        return ans

a.t: O(n^2) — for each of n middle indices we rebuild counters and multiply O(distinct) linear factors into a constant-size grid.
a.sp: O(n) — the two counter maps per iteration.

w: This is the intended hardness: the trap is forgetting that the middle index demands exactly 2 elements per side (a naive 'count any 5-subsequence containing enough copies of v' overcounts badly). Verify the case table against [1,2,2,3,3,4] -> 4 and all-equal arrays -> C(n-1, 4) adjusted per middle. Pitfalls: values can be negative/large (hash them, do not bucket by array index), and intermediate products like c2(Lv)*c2(B) reach ~2.5e11, requiring 64-bit types. Follow-up: the size-7 version, or counting subsequences where the mode is unique but not necessarily in the middle.
